USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Subset Sum. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is 3-SAT and TARGET is Subset Sum. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = ThreeSat
3-SAT.

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[l1, l2, l3], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * Every clause has exactly 3 literals on 3 different variables, so a
    clause may not repeat a variable or contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes), for any m,
including m = 0. A formula with clauses needs m >= 3.

TARGET = SubsetSum
Subset Sum.

Instance: {"numbers": [a1, a2, ...], "target": t}
  * The numbers are non-negative integers of any size; values may repeat.
  * The target is any integer.

Yes iff some sub-list of the numbers (each position used at most once)
sums to exactly t.

Edge cases: t = 0 is always yes (the empty sub-list). t < 0 is always
no. An empty list is yes only for t = 0.

WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-d0ougo1j

    reduce(instance) -> instance

The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

{"command":"cd /tmp/reduction-d0ougo1j && cat > reduce.py <<'EOF'
"""Polynomial-time reduction from 3-SAT to Subset Sum.

Construction (standard digit / base-10 encoding)
------------------------------------------------
Let the formula have m variables and k clauses.  Use m + k decimal
"columns": column i (1 <= i <= m) is the variable column of variable i and
column m + j (1 <= j <= k) is the clause column of clause j.

Numbers (all non-negative integers, base 10, so no carries can occur):

  * For every variable i, two numbers:
        T_i = 10^i + sum over clauses j containing literal +i of 10^(m+j)
        F_i = 10^i + sum over clauses j containing literal -i of 10^(m+j)
    Thus T_i/F_i each contribute 1 to variable column i, and 1 to the
    clause columns of the clauses they satisfy.

  * For every clause j, two identical numbers 10^(m+j).  They can top a
    clause column up by at most 2.

Target:
        t = sum_{i=1..m} 10^i  +  3 * sum_{j=1..k} 10^(m+j)

Why it works
------------
No column ever exceeds 5 (variable columns get at most 1, clause columns
get at most 3 from the literals plus 2 from the clause numbers), so there
are no carries and each column must match exactly.

Variable column i must equal 1, so exactly one of T_i, F_i is chosen:
that is the truth value of variable i.  Clause column j then contains the
number s of true literals of clause j (0..3) plus c, where c in {0,1,2}
is the number of clause-j filler numbers chosen.  The column must equal 3,
which is possible iff s >= 1, i.e. iff the clause is satisfied.  Hence a
subset summing to the target exists exactly when the formula is
satisfiable.

Edge cases: with no clauses the target is sum_i 10^i and picking one of
T_i/F_i per variable hits it (yes); with m = 0 and no clauses the target
is 0 and the empty sub-list works (yes).
"""


def reduce(instance):
    num_vars = instance["num_vars"]
    clauses = instance["clauses"]
    num_clauses = len(clauses)

    base = 10
    numbers = []

    # Variable numbers: one true-number and one false-number per variable.
    for var in range(1, num_vars + 1):
        true_num = base ** var
        false_num = base ** var
        for j, clause in enumerate(clauses):
            column = base ** (num_vars + 1 + j)
            if var in clause:
                true_num += column
            if -var in clause:
                false_num += column
